title: Farid of Pakpattan
hookLine: Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of the Punjab centuries before Nanak, whose Punjabi verses the Gurus treasured

cards: A shrine stands in a small town in what is now Pakistan, and visitors of more than one faith come to it. The man remembered there was a Muslim holy man, a Sufi of the Punjab, who lived centuries before Guru Nanak.
He wrote in the Punjabi of the villages, the language of the Guru Granth Sahib's heartland. And the Gurus kept his verses in their own book. Today, Farid of Pakpattan.

teach.b: Sheikh Farid, often called Baba Farid, was a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, of the Chishti order.
He settled in a river town called Ajodhan, later renamed Pakpattan, and tradition says he taught, fasted, prayed and fed whoever came there.

People called him Ganjshakar, treasury of sugar; there are many stories about why, and nobody can say which is true. What matters here is his language. Learned writing of his day was in Persian or Arabic.
Farid's couplets are in the villagers' own Punjabi, and tradition counts them among the earliest poetry in the language. Hence the first Punjabi voice.
The Guru Granth Sahib holds four of his hymns and more than a hundred saloks under his name. Sikh tradition says Guru Nanak met one of Farid's successors at Pakpattan and brought his verses home.
Scholars debate whether every salok is by Farid himself or partly by later Sheikhs of his line who used his name. Either way, the Gurus heard their own teaching in them.
Here's one, in paraphrase: don't speak even one harsh word, for the True Lord lives in everyone.
Don't break anyone's heart; every heart is a priceless jewel.
A Muslim saint in a Sikh book, speaking the people's language about the jewel in every heart: truth having many singers, again.

how: Farid's saloks and hymns are sung in Sikh kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib; his shrine at Pakpattan, in Pakistan's Punjab, is visited by people of many faiths.

games.q: you're a Sufi teacher in Farid's Punjab, and learned writing is in Persian. what language do Farid's couplets use?
games.why: Farid's couplets are in ordinary people's own Punjabi, and he's remembered as the first Punjabi voice.

practice: Say Farid's line slowly in your mind: don't break anyone's heart; every heart is a priceless jewel.

Then picture one heart you might bruise today without meaning to, someone rushed, someone tired, someone who annoys you, and see it as a jewel, easy to scratch, impossible to replace. Let the breath be soft.

wordCard.voice: Ganjshakar, treasury of sugar, Farid's own title. Baba Farid, the Chishti Sufi whose Punjabi couplets, counted among the earliest in the language, the Gurus placed in the Granth.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Farid, an Arabic name meaning unique, matchless; his saloks begin fareedaa, O Farid.

carryVoice: Your line: the first punjabi voice. Older than the Gurus, and kept by them. Two hundred fifty-eight days in.
